comment: The dev-loop agent registry, read by BOTH loop.sh and bin/doctor.ts.
It is one file because it was previously two: `DEV_AGENT_IDS` in loop.sh and
`DEV_AGENTS` in bin/doctor.ts, each an independent copy of the same list in the same
order. doctor.ts's own comment depended on that order ('loop.sh takes the first match
in DEV_AGENTS order'), so the two had to agree, and nothing checked that they did — a
vendor added to one would have been advertised or auto-detected inconsistently by the
other, silently.
THE CONTRACT AN ENTRY MUST SATISFY. These are the only things the loop assumes, and
therefore everything needed to add a vendor:
1. reads its instructions from STDIN (never argv: the cycle prompt is long, and
argv leaks it into the process table)
2. can create and edit files in the repo, and run the repo's own commands
3. runs to completion non-interactively, with no approval prompt
4. exits 0 on success and nonzero on failure — a nonzero exit fails the cycle,
because partial output is not evidence the requested work completed
Anything meeting that contract works whether or not it is listed here: AI_AGENT_CMD
takes an arbitrary command. This list exists so the common cases need no
configuration, NOT to restrict the field. There is no `order` field: the ORDER OF THE
`agents` ARRAY below is the auto-detect precedence when no AI_AGENT is set; it is a
tie-break among installed agents, not a ranking.
The bare `claude` entry is only an auto-detect default. `--permission-mode acceptEdits`
approves file edits, not shell commands, so a headless run cannot run npm/git unless the
operator's own Claude settings allow them. For unattended Claude runs set
AI_AGENT_CMD=agents/claude-headless-worker.sh (docs/afk_loop.md).
Flags are operator-verifiable: CLIs change, and a wrong flag here should be a
one-line fix rather than a reason to distrust the loop. Confirm yours once with
`AI_AGENT=<id> AI_LOOP_MAX_CYCLES=1 ./loop.sh`.
Placeholders in `command` never splice their VALUE into the command string. loop.sh
runs that string with `bash -c`, so each placeholder becomes a quoted positional
reference and the value arrives as a separate argument that is never parsed as
shell (a checkout path with a space or `;` or `$(...)` stays one word):
{CWD}     — "$1", the repo root the cycle runs in
{SANDBOX} — "$2", the value of AI_CODEX_SANDBOX, defaulting to workspace-write
